title: Caring for the earth
hook: the earth is the great mother of the Japji's last salok

segments.voice: Yesterday, kudrat: Guru Nanak giving himself to the One who dwells in creation. Your line was he dwells in nature. What living thing did you look at a beat longer? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-nine.

Sikhs who recite the Japji in the morning end on its last salok, and it sounds less like the end of a hymn than like a family introduction. Here is your teacher. Here is your father. Here is your mother. And the names that follow aren't people. They're air, and water, and the ground under your feet. For someone who has just finished a long climb through the Japji's thought, it's a strange and lovely way to come down: back onto the earth, as a child comes back into a lap. Today, that last salok, and what it asks of the people who say it.
screen: `THE JAPJI'S LAST SALOK.` → `A FAMILY INTRODUCTION.` → `AIR, WATER, EARTH.`

segments.voice: First, the family. In Gurmukhi the salok opens pavan guru, pani pita, mata dharat mahat. In paraphrase: air is the Guru, water is the father, and the earth is the great mother. Not a vague nature. A family, with roles. Air teaches, the way breath and sound carry the Word. Water gives life the way a father is said to. And the earth holds and feeds, the great mother. Second, the lap. The salok goes on, in paraphrase: day and night are the two nurses, and the whole world plays in their lap. The planet becomes a nursery, the turning of light and dark like two caregivers taking shifts. Third, the reckoning. Then the tone changes. Good and bad deeds are read out before the Lord, and each person's own actions bring them near or send them far. The child playing in the lap is also answerable for how it plays. Fourth, what a family member does. You don't strip your mother's house. You don't foul your father's water. If the earth is the great mother, then caring for it isn't an extra cause bolted onto faith; it's simply how you treat family. Some Sikhs have taken the salok as the heart of environmental work, planting trees and cleaning rivers in its name. The Japji ends on the ground, among relatives, with the day's account still open.
screen: `AIR THE GURU, WATER THE FATHER.` · `DAY AND NIGHT: TWO NURSES.` · `DEEDS READ OUT.` · `YOU DON'T STRIP YOUR MOTHER'S HOUSE.` · then, large: `THE GREAT MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for one bit of earth. Settle, and breathe. Feel the air going in: the Guru, the salok says. Feel your weight on the floor or the ground beneath you: the great mother, holding you up without being asked. Stay with that for a few breaths. Then choose one small piece of earth you can care for today: a plant to water, litter to pick up, a tap left running to turn off, a scrap of compost. Hold the picture of doing it. The bell holds the time.
Caring for the earth. The Japji's last salok calls air the Guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother; caring for her is how family treats family. Today's word.
Your line: the great mother. Today, do the one thing you chose, and do it the way you'd tidy up for your own mother. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-nine.
